changelog:
[COLOR fffdb515]Artwork quality is two clear choices now[/COLOR]
-Auto is gone from the settings. It worked out the right size from Kodi's storage limit, a number buried in a file most people have never opened, so two devices with the same screen could end up asking for different things with no way to tell why. Worse, when that limit fell between two of TMDb's sizes, Auto had no choice but to jump to the full-size original: a one megabyte file downloaded and decoded to keep three hundred kilobytes.
-In its place: Standard, where you pick each of the three yourself - posters at w500 or w780, fanart at w1280 or original, episode thumbnails at w300 or original. Or Maximum, which is everything at original size. There is no middle step to offer in fanart or thumbnails because TMDb publishes nothing between w1280 and original, or between w300 and original, but the two ends are a real choice and they are yours to make.
-Neither profile looks at your screen, and that is deliberate. The 1080 and 4K screens the add-on carries are its own dialogs and they switch at 2160 pixels tall, so they say nothing about what a panel can actually draw - a tablet running at 2800x1752 uses the 1080 set and still draws a 1752 pixel poster. Tying quality to that would promise a match that does not exist. If you want Standard on a 4K TV that is your call, and if you want Maximum on a small screen that is your call too.
-The display test is where you find out whether your choice suits you. It now says plainly when Standard is too small for a 4K panel, when you are downloading more than Kodi will keep, and when your storage limit has room you are not using. It tells you; it does not decide for you.
-Anyone on Auto today lands on Standard, which is the intended replacement. Anyone on Original stays where they are.
[COLOR fffdb515]Alternate poster rotation actually works now[/COLOR]
-Two functions were being called that had never been written. The poster rotation one sat inside a silent catch, so rotating between TMDb's alternate posters has never worked in any release - it failed on every title without leaving a trace in the log. The English title one was not protected at all and would break a title's details outright when Prefer English titles was on with the interface in another language. Both are now implemented, working off data the add-on already receives, so there is not one extra request.
-English titles are worked out the reliable way first: when a film or show is originally in English, its original title is the English one. Only when it is not does it fall back to alternative titles, and there it accepts only US and UK entries and ignores working titles and DVD titles, which are not what a film is known by.
[COLOR fffdb515]Artwork cleanup on a schedule that stays out of the way[/COLOR]
-The cleanup used to check the moment the service started and then hourly, on a fixed seven day rule. If the seventh day happened to land on a start-up, it began deleting right on top of the catalogue refresh.
-Now the first pass waits half an hour after start-up, by which time the catalogue has been done for a very long time, and then repeats once a day for as long as Kodi stays open. It covers posters, fanart and stills, and it runs without a word.
-How long artwork has to go unused before it goes is now yours to set: one, three or seven days. Seven stays the default so nobody's behaviour changes without being asked.
-It still stops the instant you start watching something. It now also skips the rows Kodi keeps for artwork it never actually downloaded - on a home screen full of widgets there are thousands of those, and asking about each one was most of the cost of a pass. There is a cap per pass so a large backlog is spread out rather than run as a marathon, and the log records how many went, how many megabytes came back and how long it took.
-Worth knowing: artwork is deleted by when it was last used, not by when it arrived. Posters on your home screen and in the lists you open daily refresh that date every time, so they are never touched. What goes is the tail of things looked at once and never opened again.
